To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
citizens in developing countries prefer PTAs that liberalize trade, but not to the same extent as economists would expect.

(1) preferences for trade liberalization in the three countries are driven not only by standard economic logic but also by non-economic factors such as sympathy/ antipathy towards particular countries and environmental/labor rights concerns; (2) preferences for trade policy are surprisingly consistent across the three countries, despite strong macro-economic and political differences between them; and (3) the main differences between the countries are in the level of support for trade policy and in the importance of non-economic considerations

(i) citizens in developing countries are more concerned with the social and environmental implications of trade liberalization than the economic implications and (ii) they prefer a PTA that is limited in its scope and scale, that includes environmental and labor rights provisions, and that does not include labor market access.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how citizens in developing countries evaluate trade liberalization and what they want in terms of the content of trade agreements.
the following questions. What kinds of trade liberalisation agreements do people want? How does this vary by country, and how do different
the question of whether and how trade liberalization is perceived as an opportunity or a threat by citizens in developing countries.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
citizens in developing countries prefer a PTA that liberalizes trade in goods and services and allows labor mobility, but not one that imposes environmental and labor standards.
the preferences of the populations of these three countries for PTAs with different characteristics are not very different.
citizens in developing countries want trade liberalization, but they want to liberalize selectively and with safeguards for the poor and the environment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

people in the surveyed countries are in favor of trade liberalization agreements that are limited to goods and services trade (and not including labor market access), are limited in scope to a small number of countries (and not including the whole world), and that include environmental and labor standards.
the public in developing countries is more open to free trade than is commonly assumed, but that they are also very concerned about non-economic aspects of trade liberalization.
the citizens of Costa Rica, Nicaragua and Vietnam want trade liberalization, but not free trade.
The main takeaway from our work is that
citizens in the Global South are not only concerned about trade policy but also that their preferences are not necessarily driven by economic self-interest.

the content of PTAs is of central concern to citizens in developing countries, and that citizens in these countries are willing to pay a price for PTAs that include provisions on labor rights and labor market access.
the design of PTAs is not a purely economic matter, but rather a political one, and that the political context is not necessarily a major impediment to reaching agreement.
